The Atacama Desert is a plateau in South America, mostly in northern Chile, with parts reaching toward southern Peru. It is often called the driest non-polar desert in the world. Some weather stations in its interior have gone many years without significant rain. The desert forms a narrow north-south strip along the Pacific coast, between the ocean to the west and the Andes Mountains to the east.

The Atacama covers roughly 105,000 square kilometers (about 41,000 square miles), though broader definitions include the surrounding arid lands. Three things cause the dryness. The cold Humboldt Current offshore suppresses evaporation and cloud formation, the subtropical high-pressure system inhibits precipitation, and the Andes block moist air from the Amazon Basin. Much of the region gets only a few millimeters of rain a year, and some central areas can go decades without measurable precipitation.

Vegetation is sparse in the hyper-arid core, but cacti, shrubs, and hardy grasses grow in less extreme zones. Coastal fog, known locally as camanchaca, supplies moisture to some ecosystems. Insects, reptiles, birds, and mammals adapted to aridity live there, and high-altitude wetlands and salt flats support flamingos and other Andean species.

Indigenous peoples have long lived in the desert, among them the Atacameño, or Likan Antai, who built settlements in oases and river valleys. The region came under Spanish control with European colonization. In the 19th century, deposits of nitrates, copper, and other minerals made it economically important. Disputes over these resources contributed to the War of the Pacific (1879-1884), after which Chile gained extensive desert territories that Peru and Bolivia had held.

Mining is still a major activity, especially for copper and lithium. The Atacama is also important for astronomy. High elevation, minimal cloud cover, low humidity, and little light pollution make it one of the best places on Earth for observing the sky. Observatories in or near the region include the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and several facilities on Cerro Paranal and La Silla.

The desert also draws tourists and researchers. Its landscapes include salt flats, volcanoes, geysers, and eroded rock formations. Its dry, Mars-like conditions have led researchers to use it as an analog environment for testing space exploration technology and studying the limits of life in extreme environments.

Moving to a new city feels, at first, like borrowing a life that belongs to someone braver than I am. The decision usually starts out abstract: a job offer, a school, a relationship, a vague hunger to start over. On paper the move looks clean and purposeful. In practice it is cardboard boxes, forwarded mail, directions in a robotic GPS voice, and the shock of waking in a room where the light falls differently on the wall. The pleasures and the costs arrive together, and it is hard to pull them apart.

The best thing about a new city may be the permission it gives you to start over as someone else. At home, repetition settles your identity. You are someone's child, someone's friend, the person who orders the usual at the coffee shop or avoids certain streets because of old memories. In a new city nobody knows those stories unless you tell them. That can be lonely, and it can also be a relief. You can be more social or more private. You can try new routines and new neighborhoods, even a different version of your personality. Nobody there is checking who you used to be.

Discovery is the other pleasure, and it is a simple one. Buying groceries becomes a minor expedition. You notice the architecture, the slang, the weather, how people wait in line or greet strangers. You learn where the best bread is, which park is quietest at dusk, which train platform fills up fastest in the rain. These details pile up slowly, and each one makes the place feel less like a map and more like home. Daily life, it turns out, is not fixed, and it can still surprise you.

The costs are real too, and they are harder to total than rent and a moving truck. Homesickness is the obvious one, though the word sounds too soft for what it can be. It means missing people and also missing the version of yourself that existed effortlessly among them. In the old city you knew how to belong without thinking. In the new one belonging is work. You have to build a life nearly from scratch: a doctor, a mechanic, a favorite café, a person to call when something breaks. Even small errands wear you out when there is no familiarity to cushion them.

Distance has its own arithmetic. Moving often means accepting that love gets less convenient. Friendships that proximity once sustained have to survive on texts, scheduled calls, and the occasional expensive visit. Family milestones happen without you, or you go back and find that "home" kept changing while you were gone. The city you left does not wait, preserved for your return. It moves on, the way you do. That realization carries grief.

Perhaps that is part of what moving is worth: you cannot expand a life without unsettling it. The move gives you freedom and novelty, and it charges you in loneliness, uncertainty, and loss. You agree to that exchange when you go. If you are lucky, the strange streets become your streets over time. The costs do not disappear, but after a while they feel less like penalties.

**Hospital Network Reports Data Breach Affecting Thousands of Patients**

A large regional hospital network said Tuesday it is investigating a data breach that may have exposed the personal and medical information of thousands of patients.

The network operates several hospitals, outpatient clinics, and specialty care centers across the region. Officials said in a statement that it detected suspicious activity in its computer systems earlier this month. They said the network moved quickly to contain the incident, began an internal investigation, and hired outside cybersecurity experts to determine the scope of the breach.

Early findings suggest unauthorized actors may have accessed patient records containing names, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers, medical record numbers, and insurance details. In some cases the records also held limited clinical information. Officials said they have found no evidence that financial account or payment card data was compromised. The investigation is ongoing.

“We take the privacy and security of our patients’ information extremely seriously,” the hospital network said in its statement. “Upon discovering this issue, we immediately implemented containment measures, notified law enforcement, and began working with leading forensic specialists to assess what information may have been affected.”

The network did not say how many patients are involved but called the breach “significant.” It expects to notify affected people by mail in the coming weeks and will offer eligible patients complimentary credit monitoring and identity protection services.

Hospital operations have continued. Some administrative systems were temporarily taken offline, which delayed scheduling and limited access to certain online services. Emergency departments and inpatient care were not disrupted, officials said.

Cybersecurity experts say healthcare organizations remain attractive targets for hackers because they hold so much sensitive personal and medical data. Unlike stolen credit card numbers, medical records can contain permanent identifying details that may be used for identity theft, insurance fraud, or phishing attacks.

“This type of incident can have long-lasting consequences for patients,” said one data privacy analyst not affiliated with the hospital network. “Even if clinical care is unaffected, the loss of trust can be substantial, especially when health information is involved.”

Regulators are likely to review the breach under federal health privacy rules, including the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, or HIPAA. The law requires covered entities to safeguard patient information and to notify individuals when certain breaches occur.

Patients are advised to watch for unexpected bills, insurance statements, or suspicious emails and phone calls that reference their medical care. The network said it is strengthening system security, reviewing access controls, and taking steps to prevent similar incidents.

A good teacher knows the subject, but that is only the start. Information on its own doesn't make anyone curious or confident. I think a good teacher needs patience, passion, empathy, and a way of making students feel seen. The best ones build a room where learning seems possible.

Patience comes first. Students learn at different speeds and think in different ways, and a good teacher accepts that. When a student struggles, they try another explanation or another example instead of getting frustrated. That tells the student that difficulty is not failure and that understanding sometimes takes time. For someone who already doubts themselves, it can change a great deal. A patient teacher also teaches perseverance.

Passion is next. Students can tell when a teacher cares about the material. Enthusiasm spreads. Someone who talks about literature, science, history, or math with real interest can make a hard topic come alive, and the lessons stop being a list of facts. Students see that learning can bring joy as well as obligation.

Empathy matters just as much. A good teacher remembers what it was like to be confused, nervous, or afraid of mistakes. They know students carry things nobody sees: trouble at home, stress, insecurity, loneliness, pressure to succeed. So they are kind and respectful, and they listen. They notice the student who has gone quiet or seems discouraged. Sometimes encouragement at the right moment is worth more than an explanation. A student who feels understood is more likely to speak up, take risks, and believe they can improve.

Good teachers also challenge students. Kindness doesn't mean lowering standards. Some of the most effective teachers expect a great deal because they see what their students could do. They push students to think harder, work more carefully, and aim higher than they would alone. The expectations come with support, though. These teachers demand excellence and then help students reach it.

The impact reaches past the classroom. Years later, students forget lessons, dates, and formulas, but they remember how a teacher made them feel: the one who believed in them when they doubted themselves, who sparked an interest they had never considered, who showed them their voice mattered. Teaching shapes character and possibility as well as education.

To me, a good teacher combines knowledge with humanity. They guide and challenge their students, and they help them learn about themselves as well as the world. That kind of influence can last a lifetime.

# Commit Message Style Guide

A good commit message helps teammates review a change and helps future maintainers understand the decision behind it. It also makes `git log` and `git blame` more useful when you are debugging. Follow these conventions for every commit.

## Structure

```
<subject line>

<body>

<footer>
```

Separate the subject from the body with a blank line. The body and footer are optional for trivial changes.

## Subject Line

- **Limit to 50 characters.** The hard limit is 72.
- **Use the imperative mood**: "Add retry logic," not "Added retry logic" or "Adds retry logic." A quick test: the subject should complete the sentence, "If applied, this commit will…"
- **Capitalize the first word.**
- **Omit the trailing period.**
- **Be specific.** "Fix bug" and "Update code" say nothing. "Fix null check in user lookup" does.

If your team uses prefixes such as `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, or `refactor:` (Conventional Commits), apply them consistently and keep the total length within the limit.

## Body

Use the body to explain **what changed and why**. The diff already shows how. Questions to answer:

- What problem prompted this change?
- Why did you choose this approach over alternatives?
- What side effects or limitations should reviewers know about?

Wrap lines at 72 characters. Use hyphens or asterisks for bullet points when listing discrete changes.

## Footer

Use the footer for metadata:

- Issue references: `Fixes #123`, `Refs #456`
- Breaking changes: `BREAKING CHANGE: description`
- Co-authors: `Co-authored-by: Name <email>`

## Scope of a Commit

Make each commit a single logical change. If you need "and" in your subject line, consider splitting the commit. Don't mix formatting changes with functional ones, because that makes review and reverting harder.

## Examples

**Weak:**
```
fixed stuff
```

**Strong:**

# Tbilisi

**Tbilisi** (Georgian: თბილისი), historically known as **Tiflis**, is the capital and largest city of Georgia. It lies on the banks of the Mtkvari (Kura) River and had a population of approximately 1.2 million in the early 2020s, about a third of the country's population. The city is a cultural and economic center and a transport hub in the South Caucasus.

## History

According to tradition, King Vakhtang I Gorgasali of Iberia founded the city in the 5th century AD after discovering warm sulfur springs while hunting. The name derives from the Old Georgian *tbili*, meaning "warm." His successors moved the royal seat to Tbilisi, and the city grew in importance despite repeated invasions by Persians, Byzantines, Arabs, Mongols, and Turkic dynasties.

Tbilisi prospered during the Georgian Golden Age under King David IV and Queen Tamar in the 12th and early 13th centuries, although it was later sacked several times, notably by Timur and by the Persian ruler Agha Mohammad Khan in 1795. Georgia was annexed by the Russian Empire in the early 19th century, and Tbilisi became the administrative center of the Caucasus Viceroyalty. After a brief independence from 1918 to 1921, the city became the capital of the Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic. Georgia regained independence in 1991. Since then Tbilisi has seen political upheaval, including the Rose Revolution of 2003, and considerable modernization.

## Geography and climate

The city occupies a valley surrounded by mountains and hills, at an elevation of roughly 400–770 meters above sea level. Tbilisi has a transitional climate between humid subtropical and continental, with hot summers and cool winters.

## Culture and architecture

The city's architecture is eclectic, mixing medieval, neoclassical, Art Nouveau, Soviet, and contemporary styles. The Old Town (Dzveli Tbilisi) has narrow streets, carved wooden balconies, and the sulfur baths of Abanotubani. Landmarks include the Narikala Fortress, the Metekhi Church, the Sioni Cathedral, the Holy Trinity Cathedral (Sameba), and the modern Bridge of Peace. The Kartlis Deda ("Mother of Georgia") statue overlooks the city from Sololaki Ridge.

Tbilisi's cultural institutions include the Georgian National Museum and the Rustaveli Theatre, and the city holds a number of festivals. Georgian cuisine, such as *khachapuri*, *khinkali*, and local wines, is part of the city's identity. Its nightlife and electronic music scene have also drawn international attention.

## Economy and transport

Tbilisi is the country's financial and commercial center. Its main sectors are services, tourism, trade, and manufacturing. The Tbilisi Metro, opened in 1966, is the city's main rapid transit system, supplemented by buses, minibuses, and a cable car. Tbilisi International Airport is the principal gateway to the country.

# Maplewood County school board election draws record turnout

**41 percent of registered voters cast ballots, more than double the last school board race**

MAPLEWOOD — Maplewood County voters elected three school board members Tuesday in a record turnout. Election officials said 41 percent of registered voters cast ballots, more than double the turnout of the last school board election and the highest for a stand-alone local race in the county's recorded history.

According to the County Elections Office, 38,214 of the district's 93,200 registered voters took part, compared with roughly 17 percent two years ago. Lines at several precincts stretched out the door after work. Lincoln Elementary kept its polls open 25 minutes past the scheduled 7 p.m. closing so the people already waiting could vote.

"We prepared for a busy day, but nothing like this," said Dolores Whitfield, the county's elections director. "By noon we had already surpassed the total in-person turnout from the last cycle."

The campaign was contentious. A proposed budget shortfall, plans to consolidate schools, and arguments over curriculum and class sizes dominated it. Six candidates competed for three open seats, spending was unusually high for a local race, and candidate forums were packed.

Parent groups on both sides of the consolidation debate organized door-knocking and carpools to the polls. In the fall, student volunteers from Maplewood High School ran a registration drive that added nearly 1,800 new voters to the rolls.

"I've lived here 30 years and never voted in a school board race until this year," said Marcus Delgado, 52, a father of two who waited about 20 minutes to vote at Lincoln Elementary. "Decisions about my kids' classrooms are being made, and I wanted a say."

Ruth Ann Kessler, a retired teacher, said she voted because of the consolidation plans. "Closing a school affects the whole neighborhood, not just the families who go there," she said.

In preliminary results, incumbent Priya Raman leads, followed by newcomers Thomas Berglund and Angela Ortiz, who hold the other two winning spots. Fewer than 400 votes separate third and fourth place. The elections office said it will not certify final results until provisional and mail-in ballots are counted next week.

Whitfield said her office would review the day's operations to prepare for future high-turnout elections. "This is a good problem to have," she said. "We hope it's a sign of lasting engagement."

The new board members will be sworn in at the first meeting of the new year.

Voyager 1

Voyager 1 is a robotic space probe that NASA launched on 5 September 1977 as part of the Voyager program. It was designed to study the outer Solar System. After finishing that mission it kept going, and it is now the most distant human-made object from Earth.

The Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) built the probe, and a Titan IIIE rocket carried it up from Cape Canaveral, Florida. Its twin, Voyager 2, launched first, but Voyager 1 took a faster trajectory and reached Jupiter and Saturn earlier. The mission used a rare planetary alignment that let spacecraft visit several outer planets by gravitational assist.

Voyager 1 reached Jupiter in 1979. It returned detailed images of the planet's atmosphere, including the turbulent cloud bands and the Great Red Spot. At Io it found evidence of active volcanism, the first seen anywhere beyond Earth. It also gathered data on Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto, and on Jupiter's magnetosphere and rings.

In 1980 it flew past Saturn and its moon Titan. Titan was a priority because of its dense atmosphere. Voyager 1 confirmed that the atmosphere is rich in nitrogen, but an opaque haze kept the cameras from imaging the surface. The probe also made extensive observations of Saturn's rings, moons, and magnetic environment. The Titan flyby required a trajectory that threw the spacecraft out of the plane of the Solar System, so no further planetary encounters were possible.

Voyager 1 then began an extended mission to study the outer heliosphere, the region shaped by the solar wind. In August 2012 NASA announced that it had crossed the heliopause, the boundary where the Sun's influence gives way to the interstellar medium, making it the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. Its instruments still measure charged particles, magnetic fields, and plasma there.

The probe also carries the Golden Record, a phonograph record of sounds, images, and messages meant to portray the diversity of life and culture on Earth. It was conceived as a symbolic message to anyone who might one day find it.

Voyager 1 still communicates with Earth through NASA's Deep Space Network. Its radioisotope thermoelectric generators are losing output, and the power supply is slowly declining. NASA has extended the mission several times, and the probe keeps sending back data as it moves deeper into interstellar space.

## Pivot Tables User Guide

A pivot table summarizes a large set of spreadsheet data without manual sorting, filtering, or formulas. You drag fields into place to group records, total them, and compare categories.

### When to use a pivot table
Use a pivot table to:
- Total sales by region, product, or salesperson
- Count records, such as customers or orders
- Compare values across categories
- Rearrange data without changing the original table

### Before you begin
Your source data needs:
- Rows and columns, with a single header row
- No completely blank rows or columns
- One data type in each column: dates, numbers, or text

The examples below use these columns: `Date`, `Region`, `Product`, `Salesperson`, `Units`, and `Revenue`.

### Creating a pivot table
1. Select any cell in your data range.
2. Open the **Insert** menu and choose **Pivot Table**.
3. Confirm the data range.
4. Choose where to place the pivot table: a new worksheet or an existing one.
5. Click **Create** or **OK**.

A blank pivot table and a field list appear.

### The four areas
Most pivot-table tools have four layout areas:

- **Rows**: lists categories vertically
- **Columns**: lists categories horizontally
- **Values**: shows a calculation such as sum, count, or average
- **Filters**: limits the data shown

### Building a basic pivot table
To total revenue by region:
1. Drag **Region** to **Rows**.
2. Drag **Revenue** to **Values**.

The table lists each region with its total revenue.

To compare revenue by region and product:
1. Keep **Region** in **Rows**.
2. Drag **Product** to **Columns**.
3. Keep **Revenue** in **Values**.

### Changing calculations
A value field can usually be summarized in other ways:
- Sum
- Count
- Average
- Minimum
- Maximum

To change the calculation:
1. Click the value field in the pivot table, or open the field settings.
2. Open **Value Field Settings** or **Summarize By**.
3. Choose the calculation you want.

### Filtering and sorting
To narrow or reorder the results, you can:
- Apply a report filter, such as showing only one year
- Sort row labels alphabetically or by value
- Expand or collapse grouped items

### Refreshing the pivot table
When the source data changes, refresh the pivot table:
1. Click anywhere in the pivot table.
2. Select **Refresh** from the pivot-table toolbar or context menu.

### Tips
- Give the columns in your source data clear names.
- Format numbers so they read easily, for example as currency or percentages.
- If dates do not group correctly, check that they are stored as real dates.
- Leave the source data unchanged and do your analysis in the pivot table.

# Pivot Table User Guide

## What Is a Pivot Table?

A pivot table summarizes large datasets without requiring formulas. It lets you group, count, total, and average your data, then rearrange it in seconds to view it from different angles. Use one when you need answers like "What were total sales by region?" or "How many orders did each rep close per month?"

## Before You Begin

Make sure your data is ready:

- **Include headers.** Every column needs a unique, nonblank title.
- **Avoid blank rows or columns.** These can cause the table to miss data.
- **Keep data consistent.** Each column should contain one type of information, such as dates or numbers only.

## Creating a Pivot Table

1. Click any cell inside your data range.
2. Open the **Insert** menu and choose **Pivot Table**.
3. Confirm the data range shown is correct.
4. Choose a destination: a new sheet (recommended) or an existing location.
5. Click **OK** or **Create**.

An empty pivot table appears, along with a field panel listing your column headers.

## The Four Areas

The field panel contains four boxes. Drag fields into them to build your report.

- **Rows:** Categories listed down the left side (for example, Product).
- **Columns:** Categories listed across the top (for example, Quarter).
- **Values:** The numbers being calculated (for example, Sum of Revenue).
- **Filters:** Fields that let you limit the whole table to specific items, such as a single year.

## Example

Suppose your data has columns for Region, Salesperson, Month, and Revenue. To see revenue by region and month:

1. Drag **Region** to Rows.
2. Drag **Month** to Columns.
3. Drag **Revenue** to Values.

The table now displays total revenue for each region-month combination, with grand totals along the edges.

## Changing the Calculation

By default, numeric fields are summed. To change this, click the field in the Values box, select **Value Field Settings**, and choose another function, such as Count, Average, Max, or Min. You can also display values as a percentage of the total.

## Refining Your Report

- **Sort:** Click the dropdown arrow beside a row or column label.
- **Filter:** Use the same arrow to uncheck items you want to hide.
- **Group:** Right-click dates to group them by month, quarter, or year.
- **Rearrange:** Drag fields between areas to see the data differently.

## Keeping Data Current

Pivot tables don't update automatically when source data changes. Right-click the table and select **Refresh**. If you've added new rows, you may need to update the source range under **Change Data Source**.

## Troubleshooting

- **Numbers counted instead of summed:** The column likely contains text or blanks. Clean the data and refresh.
- **Dates won't group:** Some entries may be stored as text. Convert them to true dates.

# What the Walls Remember

When I was nine, my grandmother took me to the train station in the town where she grew up. It had been closed for decades. The windows were clouded and the ticket counter had been stripped of its brass. She pressed her palm flat against the wall of the waiting room as though checking a sleeping animal for breath. "I left for the city from this bench," she said. "Your grandfather proposed on that platform." By any architect's measure the building was nothing special. For her, her whole life had turned on it.

I think about that whenever someone argues that old buildings are obstacles, expensive to maintain and awkward to retrofit, standing where something shinier could go. The argument isn't foolish. Old buildings leak. They resist wiring. They often fail modern codes, and sentiment won't pay for a new roof. I don't think every old structure deserves rescue, and surviving doesn't make a building sacred.

Some do deserve it, though, and I think the reasons are practical as well as sentimental.

Old buildings hold a kind of memory no archive can copy. A photograph shows how a street looked. A building lets you stand inside the proportions people once took for normal: you feel how low the ceilings were, how narrow the stairs, how much the light depended on windows rather than switches. History stops being abstract when you have to duck through its doorway.

They also carry craftsmanship we mostly can't afford anymore. The library in my hometown is a century old, and I haunted it as a teenager. Someone had carved tiny acorns into the banister. Nobody required it, and no budget meeting would approve it today. Generations of restless kids ran their hands over those acorns anyway, and I suspect it taught us, without anyone saying so, that ordinary places could be made with care.

Then there's continuity. A neighborhood built entirely of new construction can feel weightless, like a stage set waiting for a story. Old buildings make a place feel lived in. A newcomer and a lifelong resident can share a landmark even if they remember it differently, and that shared reference point holds a community together more than we notice. It is also much easier to lose than to rebuild.

There's also plain waste. As preservationists like to say, the greenest building is often the one already standing. Demolition throws away the energy and materials built into it and fills landfills besides.

The train station was eventually torn down for a parking lot. Last year I drove through town and tried to find where the bench had been. I couldn't. The asphalt was smooth, the painted lines were crisp, and nothing showed that a proposal or a departure had ever happened there.

Buildings are worth keeping because they hold the places where our lives took shape. Once one is gone, so is the bench, and so is the proof.

Old buildings leak. They resist wiring. They often fail modern codes, and sentiment won't pay for a new roof. I don't think every old structure deserves rescue, and surviving doesn't make a building sacred.

Some do deserve it, though, and I think the reasons are practical as well as sentimental.

Old buildings hold a kind of memory no archive can copy. A photograph shows how a street looked. A building lets you stand inside the proportions people once took for normal: you feel how low the ceilings were, how narrow the stairs, how much the light depended on windows rather than switches. History stops being abstract when you have to duck through its doorway.

Nobody required it, and no budget meeting would approve it today. Generations of restless kids ran their hands over those acorns anyway, and I suspect it taught us, without anyone saying so, that ordinary places could be made with care.

A newcomer and a lifelong resident can share a landmark even if they remember it differently, and that shared reference point holds a community together more than we notice. It is also much easier to lose than to rebuild.

There's also plain waste. As preservationists like to say, the greenest building is often the one already standing. Demolition throws away the energy and materials built into it and fills landfills besides.

The train station was eventually torn down for a parking lot. Last year I drove through town and tried to find where the bench had been. I couldn't. The asphalt was smooth, the painted lines were crisp, and nothing showed that a proposal or a departure had ever happened there.

Buildings are worth keeping because they hold the places where our lives took shape. Once one is gone, so is the bench, and so is the proof.

# Transit Strike Halts Buses and Trains, Leaving Thousands of Commuters Stranded

**Union rejects final offer as talks collapse overnight; city braces for second day of disruption**

Hundreds of thousands of commuters scrambled for alternatives Monday after public-transit workers walked off the job at dawn, shutting down bus and rail service across the metropolitan region.

The Metro Transit Workers Union, which represents roughly 8,200 drivers, mechanics, and station staff, began the strike at 4 a.m. after contract negotiations with the Regional Transit Authority broke down late Sunday. It is the first systemwide work stoppage in 14 years.

"We didn't want to be here," said union president Dolores Reyes, speaking from a picket line outside the Eastside bus depot. "But workers who keep this city moving can't be asked to fall behind on rent while costs rise every year."

The union is seeking a 9 percent wage increase over three years, stronger protections against assaults on drivers, and limits on mandatory overtime. Transit officials countered with a 5 percent raise and said they could not meet the remaining demands without raising fares or cutting routes.

"Our offer was fair and fiscally responsible," Authority spokesperson Martin Vail said in a statement. "We remain at the table and urge the union to return to negotiations so riders can get back to their lives."

Highways clogged before sunrise, with traffic officials reporting delays up to 70 percent longer than normal. Ride-share prices surged, and bike-share stations in the downtown core were emptied by 8 a.m. Several major employers encouraged staff to work from home.

At Central Station, normally packed with morning travelers, a handful of people stood reading posted closure notices. Marcus Hill, a hospital cafeteria worker, said he had walked two miles before finding a friend to drive him the rest of the way.

"I support the drivers, I really do," Hill said. "But I can't afford to miss shifts either. I'm stuck in the middle."

Schools reported higher-than-usual absences, and the district said it would keep yellow school buses running, since those are operated by a separate contractor. Paratransit service for riders with disabilities is operating at limited capacity under an emergency agreement, though advocates say wait times have stretched beyond two hours.

Mayor Elaine Cho called on both sides to resume talks immediately and offered city staff as mediators. "Every day this continues costs working families and local businesses," she said.

Economists estimate the shutdown could cost the regional economy $30 million per day in lost productivity and sales.

No new negotiating session has been scheduled. The union said it will continue picketing until it receives a "serious proposal," while the Authority said contingency planning is underway for a prolonged stoppage.

Age is not a reason to preserve a building. A cracked wall or a faded sign does not become meaningful by surviving. The buildings worth keeping hold something beyond their years: the memory of the people who used them, the craft of the people who built them, and a record of how those people pictured their lives. Keeping them lets one generation go on talking with the next.

I think of old buildings as public memory. Families keep photo albums and letters because objects can hold feeling in a way facts cannot, and towns need the same thing. A preserved train station, schoolhouse, or church tells us more about the people who built a place than a plaque does. The width of a staircase, the hand-carved trim around a doorway, the wear in stone steps: these show that history was lived in bodies. Someone climbed those stairs every day. Someone stood in that hallway waiting for news or work, or for grief to pass. When such a building goes, part of our shared memory goes with it.

Old buildings are also beautiful in a way that is hard to reproduce. Many were built slowly, from durable materials, with ornament that reflected pride more than efficiency. Even modest ones show a human hand in uneven bricks, in wooden floors polished by decades of footsteps, in windows placed for grace as well as function. So much construction now is driven by speed and profit that these buildings are a useful reminder that usefulness and beauty need not be enemies.

There is an ethical case too. Tearing down and rebuilding is not always progress. Sometimes it is forgetting that calls itself development. Not every old building can or should be saved, because cities must change and communities need housing, safety, and accessibility. But when a building has real architectural distinction or deep cultural importance, saving it is a form of respect. It says that the people who came before us are not disposable and that the struggles and achievements that shaped a neighborhood still count. That holds most for places tied to ordinary people rather than the wealthy or famous. A factory, a corner store, or a union hall may tell a more democratic story than a mansion.

What moves me most is that preserved buildings make time feel layered instead of lost. Walking into an old library or courthouse, you feel for a moment that your own life belongs to a longer human story. The building has outlasted fashions, governments, and private worries. It has seen generations come and go, and it still stands and still needs care. Preservation at its best is humble: we are not the first people to love a place, and we will not be the last who need something solid to remember it by.

# Contributing to the docs

Thanks for helping with the docs. Whether you fix a typo or write a new tutorial, this guide shows you how to get started.

## Ways to contribute

- Fix errors: typos, broken links, outdated screenshots, or incorrect code samples.
- Improve clarity: rewrite confusing explanations or add missing context.
- Write new content: tutorials, how-to guides, and reference pages.
- Review pull requests.
- Report issues: if you spot a problem but can't fix it, open an issue.

## Getting set up

1. Fork the repository and clone your fork locally.
2. Install dependencies with `npm install`.
3. Start the local preview server with `npm run dev`.
4. Open `http://localhost:3000`. The page updates as you edit.

For small edits, you can also click Edit this page at the bottom of any page and make the change directly on GitHub.

## Making a change

1. Create a branch with a descriptive name, such as `fix-install-typo` or `add-auth-guide`.
2. Make your edits in the `docs/` directory. Files are written in Markdown.
3. Run `npm run lint` to check formatting and `npm run build` to confirm the site builds without broken links.
4. Commit with a clear message, such as `Fix incorrect flag in CLI reference`.
5. Push your branch and open a pull request.

## Style guidelines

Please follow these conventions:

- Use plain language: short sentences and little jargon.
- Address the reader as "you."
- Use active voice. Write "Run the command," not "The command should be run."
- Put code in code blocks and specify the language for syntax highlighting.
- Use sentence case for headings.
- Test every snippet before you submit it, so the examples run.
- Write descriptive link text instead of "click here."

## Structure of the docs

We organize content into four types:

- Tutorials: step-by-step lessons for beginners.
- How-to guides: solutions to specific problems.
- Reference: precise technical descriptions.
- Explanations: background and concepts.

Keep each page to one type.

## Pull request checklist

Before you submit, confirm that:

- [ ] The site builds locally without errors.
- [ ] Links and code samples work.
- [ ] Your changes follow the style guidelines.
- [ ] The PR description explains what changed and why.

## Review process

A maintainer will typically respond within a few days and may suggest edits. That's normal. Once approved, your changes are merged and published automatically.

## Community expectations

Be respectful and patient. All contributors must follow our Code of Conduct.

## Need help?

Ask in our discussion forum or comment on an issue. First-time contributors are welcome.

The **Hanseatic League** was a commercial and defensive confederation of merchant guilds and market towns in northwestern and central Europe. It dominated maritime trade in the Baltic and North Seas from the late 12th to the 17th century. At its height it linked nearly 200 towns, from London and Bruges to Novgorod and Bergen.

The League grew out of the expansion of German merchants, especially from Lübeck and Hamburg, who wanted protection and privileges while trading abroad. Lübeck, founded in 1143 between the North and Baltic Seas, became its leading city. By the 13th century, merchant communities from German-speaking towns had set up trading outposts, known as *Kontore*, in London, Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod. These held warehouses and offices and acted as legal communities that protected Hanseatic interests.

The League was not a state. It had no formal constitution, permanent army, or centralized administration, and was a loose association of towns and merchants with shared economic interests. Representatives of member cities met at assemblies called the *Hansetag* to settle commercial policy, mutual defense, and relations with foreign rulers. Membership was fluid, and cities took part to different degrees.

Its economic power rested on the exchange of regional goods. Grain, timber, wax, fur, and fish came from the east; cloth, wine, salt, and metal goods came from the west and south. Hanseatic merchants built shipping networks and standardized commercial practices, which lowered transaction costs and increased trust over long distances. When necessary, the League used embargoes and naval force to defend its privileges, as in its conflicts with Denmark in the 14th century.

The League declined gradually from the late 15th century. Stronger territorial states, trade routes shifting toward the Atlantic, Dutch and English competition, and internal divisions all weakened it. Its overseas privileges were reduced step by step, and several *Kontore* closed. Some cities still identified with the League, but by the 17th century its political significance had largely disappeared. The last *Hansetag* met in 1669.

Its mark remains in the urban culture, architecture, and commercial law of northern Europe. Lübeck, Hamburg, Bremen, and Tallinn still have brick Gothic buildings and civic traditions associated with the League. Modern historiography often treats it as an early example of transnational commercial cooperation and urban networking.

# Bike-Share FAQ

## Getting Started

**How do I rent a bike?**
Download our app and create an account. Then find a nearby station, tap "Unlock," and scan the QR code on the bike. You can also unlock bikes at station kiosks using a credit card.

**How much does it cost?**
- **Single ride:** $1 to unlock, plus $0.15 per minute
- **Day pass:** $12, with unlimited 30-minute rides for 24 hours
- **Monthly membership:** $20, with unlimited 45-minute rides
- **Annual membership:** $150, with unlimited 45-minute rides

Discounted memberships are available for students, seniors, and low-income residents. Visit our website to apply.

## Using the Service

**How long can I keep a bike?**
Ride as long as you like, but time beyond your plan's included minutes is billed at $0.15 per minute. For longer trips, dock the bike and check out another to reset your time.

**Where can I return my bike?**
Return it to any station with an open dock. Push the front wheel firmly into the dock until the light turns green. If a station is full, use the app to find the nearest one with space, and you'll receive a free 10-minute extension.

**Do I need to bring a helmet?**
Helmets aren't provided, but we recommend wearing one. Riders under 16 are required by law to wear a helmet.

**Are electric bikes available?**
Yes. E-bikes are marked with a green stripe and cost an additional $0.10 per minute. They assist you up to 20 mph.

## Safety and Problems

**What if a bike is damaged?**
Check the brakes, tires, and seat before riding. If something seems wrong, press the red "Report" button on the bike's screen or use the app. Then return it to a dock to take it out of service. You won't be charged for rides under one minute.

**What if the bike is lost or stolen?**
Lock the bike with the built-in cable lock whenever you pause. Use the "Hold" feature in the app for short stops. If a bike is lost or stolen while in your care, report it within 24 hours. Unreported losses may result in a $250 fee.

**Can I ride at night?**
Yes. Our bikes have built-in front and rear lights that activate automatically.

## Account Help

**Can I share my membership?**
No. Memberships are personal, and each account can only unlock one bike at a time. Group rides require multiple accounts.

**How do I cancel my membership?**
Go to Settings > Membership in the app and select "Cancel." Monthly plans end at the close of the billing period, and annual plans can be refunded within 14 days.

**Who do I contact for help?**
Call 555-0142, email help@citybikeshare.example, or use the in-app chat. Support is available daily from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.

## Plugin System

The editor has a plugin system for extending it without modifying the main application. Plugins can add commands, sidebar panels, language support, formatters, themes, and event-driven behavior.

### Plugin Structure

Each plugin lives in its own directory and must include a manifest file named `plugin.json`. A typical layout:

```text
my-plugin/
  plugin.json
  main.js
  README.md
  assets/
```

The `plugin.json` file defines the plugin's metadata and entry point:

```json
{
  "id": "example.hello-world",
  "name": "Hello World",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "main.js",
  "enabled": true
}
```

Required fields:

- `id`: Unique plugin identifier.
- `name`: Human-readable name.
- `version`: Plugin version.
- `main`: Entry script loaded by the editor.

Optional fields are `description`, `author`, and `dependencies`.

### Lifecycle

At startup, the editor scans the plugin directory, reads each manifest, and loads the enabled plugins. The entry script must export an `activate` function. It can also export a `deactivate` function, which the editor calls when the plugin is unloaded or the editor exits.

Example:

```js
export function activate(api) {
  api.commands.register("hello.sayHello", () => {
    api.window.showMessage("Hello from plugin!");
  });
}

export function deactivate() {
  // Clean up resources here
}
```

Use `activate` to register commands, subscribe to events, or initialize UI elements. Use `deactivate` to dispose of timers, listeners, and temporary state.

### Editor API

Plugins interact with the editor through the `api` object passed to `activate`. Common namespaces:

- `api.commands`: Register and execute commands.
- `api.window`: Show notifications, dialogs, and UI panels.
- `api.workspace`: Access open files, project folders, and settings.
- `api.editor`: Read or modify the active document.
- `api.events`: Subscribe to editor events such as file open, save, or cursor movement.

Example command registration:

```js
export function activate(api) {
  api.commands.register("example.insertDate", () => {
    const editor = api.editor.getActiveEditor();
    if (!editor) return;

    editor.insertText(new Date().toLocaleDateString());
  });
}
```

### Installation and Management

To install a plugin, copy its directory into the editor's `plugins/` folder or use the built-in plugin manager. Users can enable, disable, update, or remove plugins from the settings interface.

If a plugin fails to load, the editor continues starting up. Load errors, activation failures, and dependency issues are logged to the developer console.

### Best Practices

- Keep plugins focused on a single responsibility.
- Use stable, namespaced command IDs such as `author.feature.action`.
- Validate settings and handle missing editor state gracefully.
- Dispose of event listeners during deactivation.
- Avoid blocking operations during activation to keep startup fast.

## Plugin System

The editor has a plugin system for extending it without modifying the main application. Plugins can add commands, sidebar panels, language support, formatters, themes, and event-driven behavior.

### Plugin Structure

Each plugin lives in its own directory and must include a manifest file named `plugin.json`. A typical layout:

```text
my-plugin/
  plugin.json
  main.js
  README.md
  assets/
```

The `plugin.json` file defines the plugin's metadata and entry point:

```json
{
  "id": "example.hello-world",
  "name": "Hello World",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "main.js",
  "enabled": true
}
```

Required fields:

- `id`: Unique plugin identifier.
- `name`: Human-readable name.
- `version`: Plugin version.
- `main`: Entry script loaded by the editor.

Optional fields may include `description`, `author`, and `dependencies`.

### Lifecycle

At startup, the editor scans the plugin directory, reads each manifest, and loads the enabled plugins. The entry script must export an `activate` function. It can also export a `deactivate` function, which the editor calls when the plugin is unloaded or the editor exits.

Example:

```js
export function activate(api) {
  api.commands.register("hello.sayHello", () => {
    api.window.showMessage("Hello from plugin!");
  });
}

export function deactivate() {
  // Clean up resources here
}
```

Use `activate` to register commands, subscribe to events, or initialize UI elements. Use `deactivate` to dispose of timers, listeners, and temporary state.

Plugins interact with the editor through the `api` object passed to `activate`. Common namespaces:

- `api.commands`: Register and execute commands.
- `api.window`: Show notifications, dialogs, and UI panels.
- `api.workspace`: Access open files, project folders, and settings.
- `api.editor`: Read or modify the active document.
- `api.events`: Subscribe to editor events such as file open, save, or cursor movement.

```js
export function activate(api) {

    const editor = api.editor.getActiveEditor();
    if (!editor) return;

    editor.insertText(new Date().toLocaleDateString());
  });
}
```

- Validate settings and handle missing editor state gracefully.
- Dispose of event listeners during deactivation.

# Four Hours on a Train Without a Phone

Last summer my phone died on a train, and I had four hours of countryside ahead of me with nothing to look at but the window. For the first twenty minutes I was almost frantic. My hand kept going to my pocket, the way a tongue goes to a missing tooth. I counted fence posts. I reread the safety instructions above the door. I was bored, plainly.

Past a river I couldn't name, my mind quit scrambling for input and began making its own. I remembered a conversation with my grandmother that I hadn't thought of in years. I worked out how to restructure a project at work that had nagged me for weeks. For no reason I made up a whole backstory for the man asleep across the aisle. When we pulled into the station I felt rested, as though I'd been somewhere.

I think about that trip often. Boredom used to be unavoidable; it lived in waiting rooms and long car rides and the dead hour between homework and dinner. Now I can get rid of it completely, because any gap in the day can be filled with a feed or a podcast. I've gotten so good at escaping boredom that I've nearly forgotten what it does.

I believe it's a kind of housekeeping. With nothing demanding my attention, my mind turns inward and sorts. It connects things that don't obviously connect, and it surfaces worries I've been outrunning and wants I haven't admitted. My best ideas have never come while I was consuming something. They've come in the shower, or on a walk.

Boredom also shows you what you want. When I'm bored long enough, I find out what I want to do instead of what I'm being offered. As a kid, summer boredom eventually pushed me to build a fort, start a terrible comic, or take apart a broken radio. Nobody handed me those projects. They came out of an empty afternoon, and they felt like mine in a way entertainment never does.

None of this makes boredom pleasant. It's a signal, like hunger, that something in us wants engagement, and the mistake is answering it with whatever is nearest. A scroll quiets boredom the way fast food quiets hunger: the feeling goes away and the mind has been given nothing to chew on.

So I've started a small practice. I leave my phone in my bag while waiting in line. I take walks without headphones. Sometimes I sit on the porch and watch the light change on the neighbor's maple. The first few minutes itch. Then the restlessness eases, and thoughts I didn't know I was carrying start to come up.

I used to think an empty moment was a wasted one. I no longer do.

**The Weight of a Hamburger**

When I was nine, I watched my uncle slaughter a pig. I had been told to stay in the truck, and of course I didn't. I don't remember the blood. I remember the quiet afterward, and how ordinary the men became once it was done, rinsing their hands and talking about the weather. That night we ate pork shoulder. It was delicious, and I couldn't stop thinking about the pig's eyes.

I've been circling that evening for most of my adult life.

For years I avoided the question the way you avoid a bill you suspect you can't pay. I ate chicken breasts that came in plastic, shaped like nothing that had ever lived. Then I read a book about industrial farming, one of those books whose purpose is to ruin your appetite, and it worked. I became a vegetarian for three years. I was sincere and a little insufferable about it.

What I believed then, and still believe, is that suffering matters. Pigs are intelligent and social, and they feel fear. If I accept that a dog's pain counts for something, I have to explain why a pig's doesn't, and "because it tastes good" is a poor argument. Most of the meat in the world comes from animals that lived in conditions I would call cruel if I saw them applied to anything I loved. That is hard to argue around, and I've stopped trying.

But my certainty as a vegetarian has worn down, even though the arguments are as strong as they ever were. Life got more complicated. I spent a winter with relatives whose diet was largely what they raised and hunted, and their relationship to meat was nothing like mine. They knew the animals and thanked them without embarrassment. Nothing went to waste. I couldn't honestly say they were doing worse than I was, standing in a grocery aisle buying almond milk shipped from a drought-stricken valley. Every way of eating costs something, and I could see their costs more easily than mine.

I've landed, uncomfortably, somewhere in the middle. What bothers me most about modern meat is how well the killing is hidden from us. Distance makes cruelty easy. If I'm going to eat an animal, I should be willing to know where it lived and how it was killed. If I can't stand to know, that tells me something.

So now I eat meat rarely and try to know its source. I buy from a farmer whose fields I've walked through. Sometimes I fail, and I eat the convenient thing at an airport or a wedding and feel the old pang. I don't think this makes me virtuous. At most it makes me a more thoughtful participant in something I can't fully justify.

I used to want a clean answer, a rule I could follow or a principle that would let me stop thinking. I've come to distrust that wish.

I still think about the pig sometimes, and I don't take the memory as an order to stop eating. It's closer to a reminder to pay attention while I do.

Svalbard Global Seed Vault

The **Svalbard Global Seed Vault** is a seed storage facility on Spitsbergen, in Norway's Svalbard archipelago, about 1,300 kilometres from the North Pole. It opened in 2008 to hold duplicate samples of seeds from gene banks around the world. The duplicates guard against the loss of crop diversity to war, natural disasters, equipment failure, climate change, or poor management.

The vault is built into the side of Platåberget, a sandstone mountain near Longyearbyen. The remote Arctic site was chosen for political and environmental reasons. Svalbard is geologically stable, and the cold climate and surrounding permafrost help protect the seeds if the power fails. Seeds are stored at about −18 °C (0 °F), a standard temperature for long-term storage in seed banks.

Sometimes called the "doomsday vault," it is a backup repository rather than a conventional seed bank. It does not own the seeds. Under a "black box" arrangement they remain the property of the depositing institutions, and only the depositor can access its own collection. The arrangement is meant as an additional layer of security for national, regional, and international gene banks.

The Government of Norway developed the vault with the Nordic Genetic Resource Center (NordGen) and the Crop Trust. It can hold millions of seed samples from many food crops and their wild relatives, including wheat, rice, maize, barley, and beans. The collections are intended to support plant breeding, food security, and adaptation to changing environmental conditions.

In 2015, the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) became the first institution to withdraw seeds from the vault, after conflict in Syria disrupted operations at its regional gene bank. ICARDA used the withdrawn seeds to regenerate its collections and later redeposited fresh samples.

**The Weight of Paper**

After my grandmother died, I found her letters in a shoebox, rubber-banded by year. Mine were in there too, dutiful childhood notes about school and a lost tooth, which she had kept for decades. But it was her side of the correspondence I couldn't stop reading, the letters my mother had saved and passed back to me.

Nothing happens in them. The tomatoes are coming in late. Mrs. Dolan's hip is no better. It rained Tuesday, then Wednesday, then, she wrote, "it seemed to lose interest." I laughed out loud at that, alone in my kitchen, hearing her dry voice come through the slanted blue ink. She had crossed out a word and written another above it, and I could see her hesitate and decide. That small correction told me more about her than any photograph.

What we lose when we stop writing letters is the evidence that someone paid attention. A letter is proof that someone sat down and held you in mind for twenty uninterrupted minutes. Nobody writes one while waiting for coffee or half-watching television. Now I send dozens of messages a day. They're quick and warm and useful, and they weigh nothing. They arrive mid-distraction and are answered mid-distraction, and almost none of them are kept.

Letters also demanded patience, and the patience shaped what people said. You couldn't fire off a feeling and retract it ten seconds later. You had to let a thought finish itself, and sometimes in the finishing it changed. My grandfather, I learned from the shoebox, once wrote three pages to my grandmother about a quarrel, and the last paragraph contradicts the first. He hadn't meant to forgive her when he began. The letter got him there. A text would have kept him angry, or ended the argument in a single clipped word.

Then there was the waiting. We treat waiting as pure cost now, a flaw to be engineered away. But the days between sending and receiving gave longing somewhere to live. You walked to the mailbox with a small, private hope. When something came, it had traveled to reach you. It had a smudge on one corner and the faint smell of someone else's house.

Last winter I wrote a letter to an old friend who had moved across the country. It took me an hour and a half, far longer than I expected, because I kept discovering things I hadn't realized I wanted to say. My handwriting had gone ragged from disuse. I crossed out a word and wrote another above it. When I dropped the envelope in the box, I felt oddly exposed, as though I'd handed over something I couldn't edit.

She wrote back three weeks later. I have it still, on my desk, the paper slightly creased where her hand pressed down. It says, among other things, that it has been raining, and that the rain seems to have lost interest.

# Design Proposal: Caching Layer for Web API

## Overview
This document proposes a caching layer for the web API to reduce response latency and backend load, so the API scales better. The cache will store responses to frequently requested endpoints and serve them without repeated database or downstream service calls.

## Goals
- Reduce average API response time
- Lower database and service load
- Improve throughput during traffic spikes
- Keep data freshness acceptable
- Make cache behavior observable

## Non-Goals
- Replacing the primary database
- Caching highly sensitive or user-specific data without additional controls
- Guaranteeing perfectly fresh data for all endpoints

## Architecture
The cache sits between the API application and its backend data sources. The API checks the cache first and returns a valid entry immediately. On a miss, it fetches the data from the source, returns the response, and writes it to the cache.

We recommend a distributed in-memory store such as Redis for its low latency, support for expiration, and operational maturity. A CDN or edge cache could be added later for static or public GET endpoints.

## Cache Strategy
The initial implementation will use **cache-aside**:
1. Client requests resource
2. API looks up cache key
3. On hit, return cached response
4. On miss, fetch from backend
5. Store result in cache with TTL
6. Return response

Cache-aside is simple and suits read-heavy workloads.

## Key Design
Cache keys should be deterministic and include:
- Endpoint path
- Normalized query parameters
- API version
- Relevant request context such as locale

Example:  
`v1:products:list:category=books:page=2:locale=en-US`

## Expiration and Invalidation
Each cached item gets a TTL based on how often its endpoint changes:
- Reference data: 1–24 hours
- Frequently updated entities: 1–5 minutes
- Aggregated results: 30–120 seconds

Writes that affect cached resources should invalidate them. When a product is updated, for example, its detail and listing keys should be deleted or versioned. Where exact invalidation is hard, use shorter TTLs.

## Reliability Considerations
To avoid cache stampedes, the system should support request coalescing or soft TTL with background refresh. Known missing resources may be cached negatively for a short time to cut repeated misses. If the cache is unavailable, the API must fall back to the backend.

## Security
Sensitive data should not be cached unless it is encrypted and scoped per user. Public and shared caches must exclude authenticated or personalized responses by default.

## Observability
Metrics should include:
- Cache hit rate
- Miss rate
- Eviction rate
- Latency by endpoint
- Backend request reduction

Structured logs and dashboards should be added to track how well the cache is working.

## Rollout Plan
Start with a small set of high-read, low-volatility GET endpoints. Measure hit rate and latency, then expand gradually. Starting small limits risk and shows the real impact before the cache reaches more of the API.

Library of Alexandria

The Library of Alexandria was a famous library of the ancient world and a center of scholarship in Alexandria, Egypt, during the Hellenistic period. It was tied to the Mouseion ("Temple of the Muses"), a research institution the Ptolemaic dynasty set up after the conquests of Alexander the Great. Many details are uncertain. The library has since become a symbol of learning and of cultural loss.

It was probably founded in the early 3rd century BCE, most likely under Ptolemy I Soter or his son Ptolemy II Philadelphus. The Ptolemies wanted Alexandria to lead Greek culture and scholarship, so they gathered texts from around the Mediterranean: literature, philosophy, science, mathematics, and history. Ancient sources describe active collecting. Books arriving in the city were reportedly copied, and in some cases the library kept the originals and returned the copies to their owners.

The library sat within a wider scholarly community. Resident scholars edited and compared texts, and their work helped establish critical editions of major Greek authors such as Homer. Euclid, Eratosthenes, Aristarchus of Samothrace, and Callimachus were all associated with the institution. Callimachus is traditionally credited with compiling the Pinakes, a large bibliographic catalogue often regarded as one of the earliest library catalogues.

Estimates of the library's size vary widely. Ancient and modern figures run from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand scrolls. Scholars also debate how the library was organized and how the main library related to a possible "daughter library" in the Serapeum.

The library's destruction is a well-known episode, but it probably did not happen in a single catastrophe. Ancient and later sources link its decline to Julius Caesar's campaign in Alexandria in 48 BCE, political turmoil in the Roman period, and the destruction of pagan institutions in late antiquity, especially during the 4th century CE. Most modern historians conclude that it shrank gradually over centuries rather than being wiped out all at once.

The library has come to stand for the ideal of universal knowledge and for the fragility of cultural memory. The Bibliotheca Alexandrina, inaugurated in 2002 in modern Alexandria, was conceived as a tribute to the ancient institution.

# Hanseatic League

The **Hanseatic League** (also known as the **Hansa**) was a commercial and defensive confederation of merchant guilds and market towns in Northern and Central Europe. It began in the 12th century, peaked between the 13th and 15th centuries, and dominated trade around the Baltic and North Seas. Its member cities lay mostly along the coasts of present-day Germany, Poland, the Baltic states, and neighboring regions.

## Origins

The League grew out of associations of German merchants who traveled together for protection against piracy and banditry. Lübeck, founded in 1143, became the gateway to the Baltic and the center of this development. Its 1241 agreement with Hamburg is often cited as an early milestone. Other towns joined later, among them Cologne, Bremen, Danzig (Gdańsk), Riga, and Tallinn (Reval).

## Organization

The Hansa was never a state in the modern sense. It had no standing army, permanent treasury, or formal constitution. It was a loose association governed by periodic assemblies called the *Hansetag*, which met mainly in Lübeck. Members enforced decisions through collective economic pressure such as trade embargoes, and occasionally through military action. Lübeck is generally regarded as the leading city and was often called the League's "Queen."

## Trade

Hanseatic merchants traded in bulk goods. From the east they carried timber, furs, wax, amber, grain, and rye; from the west and south they brought cloth, wine, and manufactured goods. Salted herring from Scania and salt from Lüneburg were also important. Overseas, the League kept trading posts known as *Kontore* in London (the Steelyard), Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod (the Peterhof). They had special privileges and their own rules.

## Conflicts

Rulers resented the Hansa's trading privileges, and its power brought it into conflict with them. The main one was a war with Denmark, which ended with the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370 and confirmed Hanseatic dominance in the Baltic. Competition from Dutch, English, and Scandinavian merchants later wore down its position.

## Decline

The League weakened from the late 15th century for several reasons: strong territorial states rose, trade routes shifted toward the Atlantic, Dutch commercial power grew, and members stopped pulling together. The loss of privileges, such as the closure of the Steelyard in London in 1598, cut its influence further. The last formal assembly met in 1669, though Lübeck, Hamburg, and Bremen kept the Hanseatic name for centuries.

## Legacy

The League left brick Gothic buildings across the Baltic. Hamburg and Bremen still use "Free and Hanseatic City" in their official titles. The "New Hanse" and the annual Hanseatic Days now mark that heritage.

The Dust Bowl was a period of severe dust storms and ecological disaster on the Great Plains of the United States in the 1930s, worst from 1934 to 1936. Prolonged drought, high winds, and farming practices that left the soil open to erosion caused it. Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico were among the hardest-hit states.

Deep-rooted native grasses once covered much of the Great Plains and held the soil in place. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, large areas of prairie were plowed for wheat and cattle grazing. Crop prices were high, and many farmers believed that "rain follows the plow," so cultivation spread onto marginal land. When drought set in during the early 1930s, the bare topsoil dried out and strong winds lifted it.

Storms sometimes called "black blizzards" carried clouds of soil across towns, farms, and even distant cities. One of the most famous came on April 14, 1935, remembered as Black Sunday, when a wall of dust swept across the southern Plains. The storms destroyed crops, buried machinery, and killed livestock. They also contributed to widespread respiratory problems known as "dust pneumonia."

The Dust Bowl made the Great Depression harder to bear. Farm incomes collapsed, banks failed, and many families lost their land. Hundreds of thousands of people left the Plains, especially from Oklahoma and Arkansas, for California and other western states, looking for work. They were often called "Okies," though many came from other states. John Steinbeck's *The Grapes of Wrath* later depicted their experiences.

Under President Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal, the federal government introduced conservation and relief measures. The Soil Conservation Service, established in 1935, promoted farming methods that reduced erosion: contour plowing, crop rotation, strip farming, and shelterbelts of trees. Assistance programs helped struggling farm families either relocate or stay on their land.

Rainfall gradually returned in the late 1930s, easing the worst conditions. The Dust Bowl remains one of the most significant environmental disasters in U.S. history. It is often used as an example of what unsustainable land use and climate extremes can do to agricultural systems.

# Friends I Keep Up With

When I was twelve, my best friend moved across the country, and we wrote letters. They were clumsy, full of crossed-out words and drawings in the margins. A reply took two weeks, sometimes three. I got a small thrill from seeing her handwriting in the mailbox, and I read each letter so many times that the folds went soft. Within a year we had lost touch. Distance did that then.

My own kids will never lose a friend that way, and I'm still deciding how I feel about it.

I notice how much social media has changed friendship when I try to explain it. I know what my college roommate had for dinner last night. I know her daughter lost a tooth, her mother has been ill, and she's frustrated with her job. I haven't spoken to her in four years. Is she my friend? By the old definition, probably not. By the new one she's someone I "keep up with," a category that means closeness without contact.

Some of this is good. I've watched friendships survive moves and career changes, even the ordinary drift that once ended them. A friend in another time zone sends me voice memos while she walks her dog, and I answer while I do dishes. It's not the same as sitting across from her, but it isn't nothing. When we finally see each other, we don't start from zero.

The costs have been quieter, and I've felt them more as I've gotten older. Social media makes friendship feel like a performance with an audience. I've caught myself composing a moment while I'm still inside it, angling the dinner table for a photo, thinking of a caption while a friend is mid-sentence. The experience becomes content, and my friend becomes a co-star.

Affection has gotten cheap too. A like costs nothing, and a birthday message from a platform's reminder takes four seconds. We send these tokens and feel we've done the work of caring, but real friendship has always asked for something less efficient: showing up, sitting in awkward silence, driving across town when someone's life falls apart. No app has automated that, though apps have made it feel unnecessary.

Last winter a friend I'd only ever "liked" from afar posted something vague and sad. I almost scrolled past. Instead I called her. We talked for two hours, and she cried, and I hadn't heard her actual voice in a long time. I had nearly treated her post as scenery.

That's where I've landed. Social media didn't ruin friendship, and it didn't perfect it. It made friends easier to reach and easier to neglect. What we do with that is up to us: we can treat the feed as the friendship, or use it to find our way back to the person.

I still have my friend's old letters, soft at the folds. I don't want to go back to waiting three weeks for a reply. But I'd like to write like that again, slowly, crossing things out.

By Thursday afternoon the office feels different. People still answer email, sit through meetings, and update spreadsheets, but the sharpness of Monday is gone. Conversations drift. Small tasks take longer than they should. By Friday it can feel like everyone is performing work rather than doing it. That feeling is a big part of why I've come around to the four-day week.

Sleeping in one more day would be nice, but what persuades me is that more hours at work don't reliably mean better work. In an office job, output doesn't track hours logged. Attention runs out. Creativity thins when it's overused, and tired people make sloppier decisions. We talk as if endurance were the top professional virtue, yet clarity does more for the work than sheer duration. People aren't machines, and a schedule that pretends they are gets mediocre results.

The four-day week also treats rest as something worth having instead of an indulgence. In many work cultures exhaustion is worn like a badge of honor: being overwhelmed means you're important, and being unavailable means you're needed. That logic has started to feel hollow to me. Rest is one of the conditions that make responsibility possible. An extra day could go to recovering, looking after children or parents, making a doctor's appointment without stress, reading, exercising, or just existing outside the reach of employers and inboxes. People with room to live tend to come back to work more focused and less resentful.

I think there's a moral argument as well. For generations, technology has been sold as a route to efficiency and freedom. For many workers the efficiency arrived and the freedom didn't; expectations rose instead. We can answer messages instantly, produce documents faster, and automate routine tasks, and the usual reward is more work. A four-day week would let the gains from innovation show up as time.

Not every profession can adopt the same schedule in the same way. Hospitals, schools, factories, and service industries have practical constraints, and a four-day week won't fix every workplace problem. It takes careful implementation, staffing changes, and a real commitment not to cram five days of meetings into four. Those difficulties are reasons to plan, not reasons to drop the idea.

For me this comes down to dignity. The question is whether work should consume the best of our lives or support them. I don't think people want to contribute less. They want to contribute in a way they can keep up, with enough of themselves left for everything else.

# Wildfire Forces Thousands to Evacuate Near Cedar Ridge National Park

**CEDAR FALLS, Mont.** — A fast-moving wildfire tore through dry timber along the western edge of Cedar Ridge National Park on Tuesday, forcing the evacuation of more than 3,000 residents and prompting officials to close the park to all visitors.

The blaze, named the Hollow Creek Fire, was first reported shortly after 2 p.m. Monday and has since burned an estimated 14,000 acres. Fire officials said it was zero percent contained as of Wednesday morning.

"This fire is moving faster than anything we've seen in this area in a decade," said Incident Commander Dana Whitfield at an evening briefing. "Dry fuels, low humidity, and gusting winds are all working against us."

Mandatory evacuation orders were issued for the communities of Pine Hollow, Larkspur, and parts of Cedar Falls. An additional 2,000 residents in neighboring areas were told to be ready to leave on short notice. Sheriff's deputies went door to door overnight, and emergency alerts were sent to cell phones throughout the county.

An evacuation center opened at Cedar Falls High School, where the Red Cross provided cots, meals, and information. By midday, more than 400 people had checked in. Many arrived with pets, medications, and little else.

"We had about fifteen minutes to grab what we could," said Maria Delgado, a Larkspur resident who left with her two children and their dog. "I took photo albums, documents, and clothes. You just hope the house is still there when you get back."

Park Superintendent Tom Ellery said all campgrounds and trails had been cleared and that rangers had accounted for all registered backcountry visitors. "Visitor safety is our top priority," he said. "We are also working closely with firefighters to protect historic structures, including the Ridgeline Lodge, which dates to 1932."

More than 600 firefighters, supported by helicopters and air tankers, are battling the flames. Crews have focused on building containment lines near homes and protecting power infrastructure. Two firefighters suffered minor heat-related injuries, officials said. No civilian injuries or deaths have been reported.

Smoke has drifted across the region, and health officials issued air quality warnings for three counties, urging children, older adults, and people with respiratory conditions to stay indoors.

Meteorologists said there is a slight chance of rain late Friday, though thunderstorms could also bring lightning and erratic winds.

Governor Elaine Parks declared a state of emergency Tuesday, freeing up additional state resources. Officials have not determined the cause of the fire, and an investigation is underway.

Residents can find updates and shelter information on the county emergency management website.
