# The Weight of Boxes

The first thing I noticed about my new city was how loud the silence was. In my old apartment I knew every sound: the radiator knocking, the upstairs neighbor's heavy footsteps, the bus that groaned past at 6:40 each morning. In the sublet, which smelled faintly of someone else's cooking, I lay awake listening to noises I couldn't name.

Moving is a small, voluntary amnesia. You give up your fluency. I had lived in my old city for nine years and could get around it half asleep. I knew which grocery store had good tomatoes, which streets flooded in spring, which barista would start my order when I walked in. In the new city I got lost on the way to the pharmacy, and I stood in the cereal aisle for ten minutes over brands I didn't recognize. At thirty-four, I felt like a child, which was humbling and a little absurd.

Being lost helped, though. Within a week my attention sharpened in a way it hadn't in years. I noticed the brick on my street, a warm rust that glowed at dusk. People here nodded at strangers. I took the long way everywhere because I didn't have a short way yet. At some point I had stopped really looking at things, and an unfamiliar city made me start again. Routine had worn my days down until they all felt the same.

There were smaller pleasures. The bakery owner started saving me the end pieces of the rye loaf. On Sunday mornings the river path held runners and old men with fishing rods, all sharing the same few feet of asphalt and peacefully ignoring one another. Nobody had told me about any of it. I found it by wandering, and that made it feel like mine.

The costs were real too. One Tuesday something funny happened and I reached for my phone to tell a friend, then worked out the time zones and put it down. In the second month the novelty thinned, and I saw that friendship can't be unpacked like a box. It builds slowly, through repetition and accident and just being around. I had swapped people who knew my history for people who knew only my present, and that was lonelier than I'd expected.

I've been here a year. The bus doesn't sound foreign anymore. I have a tomato place. Last month a woman at the bakery asked how my week was going, and I had a week worth describing. I still miss the old city, the way you miss a language you used to speak well.

I think homesickness is what it costs to have loved a place, and I don't regret paying it. Moving showed me I could be rebuilt, and that I was more portable than I'd feared. The boxes are long gone.

# Dust Bowl

The **Dust Bowl**, also known as the **Dirty Thirties**, was a period of severe dust storms that caused major ecological and agricultural damage to the American and Canadian prairie lands during the 1930s. Severe drought and decades of farming without techniques to prevent wind erosion, such as crop rotation, cover crops, and terracing, caused the storms.

## Background

During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, settlers moved onto the Great Plains in large numbers, encouraged by the Homestead Acts and by unusually wet weather in the early 1900s. The native deep-rooted prairie grasses were plowed under to plant wheat. High wheat prices during and after World War I accelerated this expansion, and gasoline-powered tractors and combines let farmers cultivate far more land than before. Millions of acres of grassland became cropland, leaving the soil exposed.

## Drought and storms

A series of droughts began in 1930 and recurred in waves through 1936 and again in 1939–1940. With the grasses that once anchored the soil gone, high winds lifted the dry topsoil into enormous clouds. The most severe region included the panhandles of Texas and Oklahoma, as well as parts of western Kansas, eastern Colorado, and northeastern New Mexico.

On **April 14, 1935**, remembered as "Black Sunday," a massive storm carried dust across the southern plains and turned day into night. The following day, journalist Robert Geiger used the term "Dust Bowl" in a news dispatch, and the name stuck. Some storms carried dust as far as Washington, D.C., and ships in the Atlantic Ocean.

## Human impact

The storms damaged crops, buried farm equipment, and killed livestock. Many residents developed "dust pneumonia" and other respiratory illnesses. Combined with the economic hardship of the Great Depression, the crisis forced many families to leave their farms. Roughly 3.5 million people moved out of the Plains states in the 1930s, many of them to California. John Steinbeck's novel *The Grapes of Wrath* (1939), Dorothea Lange's photographs, and Woody Guthrie's songs recorded their experiences.

## Government response

The federal government established programs to address the crisis. The Soil Conservation Service, created in 1935 under Hugh Hammond Bennett, promoted soil-saving techniques including contour plowing, strip cropping, and crop rotation. The Prairie States Forestry Project, begun in 1934, planted millions of trees across the Plains as windbreaks known as shelterbelts. The Taylor Grazing Act of 1934 also regulated grazing on public lands.

## Legacy

Rainfall returned in late 1939, ending the drought. The Dust Bowl is among the worst environmental disasters in American history, and it influenced later soil conservation policy and farming practice.

The Erie Canal runs across New York State. It opened in 1825 and gave boats a water route from the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo, tying the Atlantic Ocean to the Great Lakes. Freight costs fell, settlement of the West sped up, and the canal helped New York City become the nation's leading port.

Before the canal, moving goods and people across the Appalachians was slow and expensive, and often unreliable. The canal was proposed in the early 19th century to fix that. Governor DeWitt Clinton became its leading political advocate. Critics mocked the project as "Clinton's Ditch." Construction began in 1817. Thousands of laborers, many of them immigrants, cleared forests, dug the channel, and built aqueducts and locks across difficult terrain.

As first built, the canal was about 363 miles (584 km) long, 40 feet (12 m) wide, and 4 feet (1.2 m) deep. Its 83 locks let boats climb more than 500 feet (150 m) between the Hudson River and Lake Erie. It officially opened on October 26, 1825. Clinton marked the occasion with the "Wedding of the Waters," a ceremonial trip from Buffalo to New York Harbor, where water from Lake Erie was poured into the Atlantic Ocean.

The canal quickly became one of North America's main transportation corridors. Freight rates between the Midwest and the East Coast fell sharply, and shipping agricultural products, raw materials, and manufactured goods got cheaper. Syracuse, Rochester, Utica, and Buffalo grew rapidly. It also drew migrants into western New York, Ohio, Indiana, and other parts of the Old Northwest.

The canal was enlarged several times during the 19th century. The New York State Barge Canal System, which opened in 1918, absorbed much of the original route and added canalized rivers and new cuts. Railroads and highways later reduced its commercial use.

Today the canal is used mainly for recreation, tourism, and heritage.

I used to think intelligence was mostly memory and discipline, with a little talent on top. Learning a second language as an adult changed that. I expected to climb steadily from confusion to fluency, picking up grammar rules and vocabulary the way you pick up tools. What I got was a long stretch of being a beginner again.

As a child, I never noticed how much of life runs on language. My first one simply worked. I joked, apologized, complained and told stories without effort. In the second language, even simple exchanges felt heavy. I would have a thought in full color and find I only had the words to say it in black and white. Someone who felt quick and articulate in one language came across as hesitant and plain in the other. I hadn't realized how much of what I called "myself" depended on expressing it easily.

It made me more patient, with myself and with other people. Once you have struggled to ask where the bathroom is, ordered the wrong food, or misunderstood a question and answered it confidently anyway, you judge everyone else's attempts more kindly. I started noticing how many people live, work and raise families in a language that isn't fully theirs. I had admired bilingual people before, but only in the abstract. Now I see it as daily courage.

I also learned that embarrassment is survivable. Adults tend to avoid anything that makes them look foolish. Children get no choice. They are corrected and misunderstood all day, and they keep going. Adults guard their competence like something breakable. Learning another language made me speak badly, mispronounce words and forget vocabulary I had supposedly already learned, and I could hear exactly where my mouth and memory ran out. That was frustrating at first. Then it got freeing. Improvement came from putting up with mistakes.

The biggest surprise was how it changed my listening. In my native language I mostly listen for meaning. In the second I listen for structure, tone, rhythm and intention, for what is said, what is implied and what I might have missed. That habit followed me back into my first language. I assume less now and ask more, and I know that understanding another person never happens as automatically as it seems.

Growth is awkward, and being a beginner again turned out to mean paying attention.

Perhaps most unexpectedly, it changed the way I listen. In my native language, I often listen for meaning alone. In a second language, I listen for structure, tone, rhythm and intention. I pay attention to what is said, what is implied, and what I might have missed. That habit followed me back into my first language. I assume less now and ask more, and I know that understanding another person is never as automatic as it seems.

Growth is awkward, and being a beginner again turned out to mean paying attention.

**Record Turnout in Riverton School-Board Election**

Voters turned out in record numbers Tuesday for the Riverton School Board election. The office usually draws little attention outside education circles.

According to the Riverton County Elections Office, more than 18,400 ballots were cast, about 46 percent of the district's registered voters. Officials said it was the highest turnout ever recorded for a stand-alone school-board election in the community, beating the previous mark, set in 2017, by nearly 5,000 votes.

Election workers reported steady lines all day at polling sites across the district, heaviest in the morning and again after work. Early voting and absentee ballots also rose sharply.

"This is the kind of civic engagement every local government hopes to see," said County Elections Director Marisol Vega. "School-board elections typically bring in a smaller slice of the electorate, so this level of turnout is remarkable."

The vote followed months of public debate over school funding, classroom overcrowding, campus safety and the district's curriculum. Candidate forums drew large audiences, and community groups on all sides ran outreach campaigns urging residents to vote.

Three seats were open. Incumbent Daniel Harper kept his, and newcomers Alicia Gomez and Trent Wallace appeared headed for victory based on unofficial returns released Tuesday night. Certified results are expected later this week. The margins were wide enough that observers said the outcome was unlikely to change.

Supporters of the winning candidates celebrated what they called a clear message from voters that the district needs both stability and fresh ideas. "People care deeply about what happens in our schools," Gomez told supporters at a gathering Tuesday evening. "Tonight's turnout shows this community is paying attention and wants a voice in the decisions affecting students and families."

Residents did not all agree on what the results meant, but many said they were glad so many people voted. Parents, teachers and retirees interviewed outside polling sites said the school board affects daily life, from academic standards to bus routes and extracurricular programs.

Superintendent Karen Liu said the turnout showed broad public investment in the district's future. "Regardless of who people supported, it is heartening to see so many residents participate," Liu said. "That kind of involvement strengthens public education."

Local analysts said the turnout could affect future elections, because school-board races can draw voters when the issues feel immediate and personal.

Startup Recalls Faulty Home Battery After Overheating Reports

VoltNest Energy, a home energy startup, is recalling about 8,200 units of its PowerVault S1 residential battery after reports that a defect can make the unit overheat. The company announced the voluntary recall Tuesday.

The PowerVault S1 is a wall-mounted system that stores electricity from rooftop solar panels or provides backup power during outages. It was sold in the United States through solar installers and the company's website between March 2024 and September 2026.

VoltNest said it has received 27 reports of overheating. Five involved minor property damage, such as scorched walls and melted wiring insulation. No serious injuries have been reported, though two customers sought medical evaluation for possible smoke inhalation.

The company said the problem appears to come from a manufacturing defect in a batch of lithium iron phosphate battery modules from a third-party vendor. Under certain charging conditions, an internal component can fail, and the unit can build up excess heat.

"We are acting out of an abundance of caution," VoltNest Chief Executive Maya Levin said in the statement. "Customer safety is our top priority, and we are working closely with regulators, installers and homeowners to replace affected units as quickly as possible."

Customers should shut the battery down right away using the system's main disconnect switch, and should not try to repair or remove it themselves. VoltNest will provide free inspections, software diagnostics and replacement units where necessary. It has also released a firmware update to reduce charging stress until replacements are done, but said the patch is not a substitute for the recall.

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission announced the recall with the company. It urged owners to follow VoltNest's shutdown instructions and to contact the company or their installer. Recalled units have serial numbers beginning with PVS1-24 or PVS1-25.

VoltNest, founded in 2021, is a venture-backed startup that has positioned itself as a lower-cost rival in the home battery market. It has grown quickly as demand for residential backup power has risen with more frequent extreme weather and strain on electric grids.

Industry analysts said the recall could temporarily slow the company's momentum, but that how it handles the response may matter more than the defect itself.

"Recalls are damaging, especially for a young brand," said energy storage analyst Daniel Cho. "But in this industry, transparency and speed matter. Homeowners need confidence that these systems are safe inside their garages and utility rooms."
